title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Store closure (Mon)
drivers.evidence: Store closed Monday; 1/5 of week lost. No similar past closures, but closure timing implies ~15% sales loss. Evidence weak, but plausible.

drivers.name: Price increase (3.97 vs 3.83)
drivers.evidence: 2026-09-28: price rise to 3.97 → 106 units (x0.80 vs baseline). Consistent pattern. Noise-adjusted effect shrunk to x0.86. Apply -10%.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline is 124.2. Halloween (Sat) typically reduces demand (median x0.79 vs baseline, noise-adjusted x1.0), so no uplift. Store closure on Monday reduces sales by ~15% (1/5 of week). Price increased 3.7% above regular (3.83 → 3.97), which historically lowers demand (2026-09-28: 106 units, x0.80 vs baseline). The classical model’s 1.00 suggests no effect, but evidence shows price hikes and closures are demand-lowering. No promotion. Adjust down for closure and price. Noise-adjusted effects are weak but consistent. Shrink toward 1.0. Final multiplier <1.0.

  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.2 | 5%-95%: 77.6 - 200.2 | 10%-90%: 89.0 - 170.1

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
